tips.title: Two meanings of pure
tips.body: **Chemistry**: a single element or compound. **Everyday**: nothing has been added. *Pure milk* is pure in the second sense and a **mixture** in the first — and the specification asks you to know both.

tips.title: A mixture melts lower as well as over a range
tips.body: Both halves earn credit, and *lower* is the one usually left out. A pure substance melts at **one specific temperature**; a mixture melts **over a range** and **below** the pure melting point.

tips.title: Rf can never exceed 1
tips.body: The denominator is how far the **solvent** moved, and the solvent **carries** the spot — so the spot cannot outrun it. An Rf above 1 is a **measuring error**, not an unusual result.

tips.title: An alloy is a formulation
tips.body: And a **mixture**, not a compound. Steel is iron with measured carbon, mixed for required hardness — purpose, measured quantities, required properties. It is the example people miss.

tips.title: Rf identifies only against a reference
tips.body: Different compounds have different Rf values **in different solvents**, so 0.45 means nothing alone. It is evidence only when matched against a reference run in the **same solvent on the same paper**.

steps.title: Mixtures
steps.body:
**A mixture consists of two or more elements or compounds not chemically combined together.**

That phrase — **not chemically combined** — is the whole definition, and everything else follows from it.

**The chemical properties of each substance in the mixture are unchanged.** Iron filings mixed with sulfur are still iron and still sulfur: the iron is still attracted to a magnet. Heat them and they **react** to form iron sulfide, which is a **compound** — and the iron is no longer magnetic, because it is no longer iron.

**Mixtures can be separated by physical processes**, and the spec names five:

- **filtration** — separates an insoluble solid from a liquid
- **crystallisation** — recovers a dissolved solid by evaporating the solvent
- **simple distillation** — separates a solvent from a solution
- **fractional distillation** — separates liquids with different boiling points
- **chromatography** — separates substances that move at different rates through a medium

**These physical processes do not involve chemical reactions and no new substances are made.** That sentence is the reason mixtures can be separated so easily: nothing has to be **undone**, only sorted.

**Compare with a compound.** Water is hydrogen and oxygen **chemically combined**, in fixed proportions, and no amount of filtering or distilling will separate them — it takes a **chemical reaction**. Air is a **mixture**, and fractional distillation separates it perfectly well.

**You should be able to suggest a suitable technique** for a given mixture, so match the method to what is being separated rather than recalling a list.

steps.title: What pure means in chemistry
steps.body:
**In chemistry, a pure substance is a single element or compound, not mixed with any other substance.**

**This is not what *pure* means in everyday language.** In ordinary use, a pure substance means one that **has had nothing added to it** — unadulterated, in its natural state. *Pure milk* means milk with nothing added.

**But milk is not pure in the chemical sense at all.** It is a mixture of water, fats, proteins and sugars. Both uses of the word are correct in their own context, and the spec asks you to know the difference.

**How to tell whether something is pure: melting and boiling points.**

> **Pure elements and compounds melt and boil at specific temperatures.**

A pure substance melts at **one sharp temperature**. An impure one melts over a **range**, and at a **lower** temperature than the pure substance would.

**So melting point and boiling point data can be used to distinguish pure substances from mixtures**, and this is a skill the spec asks for by name:

- Pure water melts at exactly **0 °C** and boils at exactly **100 °C**.
- Salt water melts **below** 0 °C and boils **above** 100 °C, and neither happens at a single sharp temperature.

**Reading the data.** Given a table of melting points, look for **one temperature** against **a range**:

- *melts at 80 °C* → pure
- *melts between 72 °C and 78 °C* → impure

That is the entire test, and it works without knowing what the substance is.

steps.title: Formulations
steps.body:
**A formulation is a mixture that has been designed as a useful product.**

That is the definition, and the important word is **designed**.

**Many products are complex mixtures in which each chemical has a particular purpose. Formulations are made by mixing the components in carefully measured quantities to ensure that the product has the required properties.**

So a formulation is not just any mixture. Muddy water is a mixture; it is not a formulation. Three things make the difference:

1. Each component has a **particular purpose**.
2. The quantities are **carefully measured**.
3. The result has **required properties** — it was made to do a job.

**The formulations the spec names:**

**fuels, cleaning agents, paints, medicines, alloys, fertilisers and foods.**

**Alloys are the one people miss.** An alloy is a mixture of metals — or of a metal and carbon, as in steel — mixed in measured proportions to give required properties such as hardness or resistance to corrosion. It is a formulation, and it is also a **mixture**, not a compound.

**Paint is the clearest illustration.** It contains a **pigment** for colour, a **binder** to hold the pigment to the surface, a **solvent** to make it spreadable, and **additives** for durability or drying time. Change the proportions and you change how the paint behaves — which is exactly why the quantities are measured.

**You should be able to identify formulations given appropriate information**, and the giveaway is a list of components **with stated purposes and quantities**. You do **not** need to know the names of components in proprietary products.

steps.title: Chromatography
steps.body:
**Chromatography can be used to separate mixtures and can give information to help identify substances.**

**It involves a stationary phase and a mobile phase.**

- The **stationary phase** does not move — in paper chromatography it is the **paper**.
- The **mobile phase** moves through it — the **solvent**.

**Separation depends on the distribution of substances between the phases.** A substance more attracted to the **mobile phase** travels **further**; one more attracted to the **stationary phase** stays **near the start**. Different substances distribute differently, so they end up in different places — which is what separates them.

**The Rf value:**

$$R_f = \frac{\text{distance moved by the substance}}{\text{distance moved by the solvent}}$$

The distance to the substance is measured from the origin to the **centre of the spot**.

**Three things follow from that equation:**

- $R_f$ has **no unit**, because it is one distance divided by another. Measure in cm or mm and you get the same number.
- $R_f$ is always **between 0 and 1**, because a spot cannot travel further than the solvent carrying it. An $R_f$ above 1 means a measuring error.
- **Different compounds have different Rf values in different solvents**, which is why $R_f$ helps **identify** a substance — but only by comparison with a known value **in the same solvent**.

**How it identifies.** Run the unknown alongside known reference substances on the same paper in the same solvent. A spot at the same height as a reference is evidence for that substance — and a mixture shows **several** spots, while a pure substance shows **one**.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Two meanings of *pure*, and the exam wants both.** In **chemistry**, pure means a **single element or compound**. In **everyday language** it means **nothing has been added**. Pure milk is pure in the second sense and a **mixture** in the first. A question asking why a food described as *pure* might not be pure to a chemist is asking for exactly this distinction.

**Melting point is the test, and the shape of the answer matters.** A pure substance melts at **one specific temperature**; a mixture melts over a **range**, and **lower**. Both halves earn credit, and the second half — *lower* — is the one usually left out.

**A formulation is designed.** Three features: each component has a **purpose**, the quantities are **carefully measured**, and the product has **required properties**. Muddy water is a mixture and not a formulation, and being able to say why shows you have the definition rather than a list of examples.

**Alloys are formulations** — and also **mixtures**, not compounds. This trips people because an alloy looks like a single material. Steel is iron mixed with measured carbon to give required hardness, which fits the definition exactly.

**Rf cannot exceed 1, and knowing why is better than remembering it.** The denominator is the distance the **solvent** moved, and the solvent is what **carries** the spot — so the spot cannot outrun it. An $R_f$ above 1 is not an unusual result; it is a measuring error, most often the solvent front measured to the wrong line.

**Rf identifies only by comparison, and only in the same solvent.** *Different compounds have different Rf values in different solvents.* So an $R_f$ of 0.45 means nothing on its own — it is evidence only when matched against a **reference run in the same solvent on the same paper**. That is why references are run alongside the unknown rather than looked up.

**One spot means pure; several mean a mixture.** This makes chromatography a **purity test** as well as a separation method — and it agrees with the melting-point test, which is a good sign that both are measuring the same underlying thing.

**Measure to the centre of the spot.** Spots spread as they travel, so the edge is ambiguous and the centre is not. It is a small instruction that carries a mark in a practical question.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **A mixture consists of two or more elements or compounds not chemically combined together.**
- **The chemical properties of each substance in a mixture are unchanged.**
- Mixtures are separated by **physical processes**: **filtration, crystallisation, simple distillation, fractional distillation, chromatography**.
- **These involve no chemical reactions, and no new substances are made.**
- **In chemistry, a pure substance is a single element or compound**, not mixed with anything else.
- **In everyday language**, *pure* means **nothing has been added** — so *pure milk* is a mixture chemically.
- **Pure elements and compounds melt and boil at specific temperatures.**
- A **mixture** melts over a **range**, and **lower** than the pure substance.
- **A formulation is a mixture that has been designed as a useful product.**
- Each component has a **purpose**, the quantities are **carefully measured**, and the product has **required properties**.
- Formulations include **fuels, cleaning agents, paints, medicines, alloys, fertilisers and foods**.
- **Chromatography** separates mixtures and helps identify substances.
- It has a **stationary phase** (the paper) and a **mobile phase** (the solvent).
- **Separation depends on the distribution of substances between the phases.**
- $R_f = \dfrac{\text{distance moved by the substance}}{\text{distance moved by the solvent}}$, measured to the **centre** of the spot.
- $R_f$ has **no unit** and is always **between 0 and 1**.
- **Different compounds have different Rf values in different solvents**, so compare only within the same solvent.
- **One spot means a pure substance; several spots mean a mixture.**

questions.prompt: Explain how chromatography separates a mixture, and how a chromatogram can be used to identify the substances present.
questions.solution: Chromatography separates a mixture using two phases. The stationary phase does not move and in paper chromatography is the paper itself, while the mobile phase is the solvent, which moves up through the paper carrying the substances with it. Separation depends on the distribution of each substance between the two phases. A substance that is more strongly attracted to the mobile phase spends more of its time moving and therefore travels a long way up the paper, whereas a substance more strongly attracted to the stationary phase spends more time held on the paper and remains near the start line. Because different substances distribute themselves differently between the phases, they finish in different positions and so are separated. The position of each spot can be expressed as an Rf value, which is the distance moved by the substance divided by the distance moved by the solvent, both measured from the origin, with the distance to the substance taken to the centre of the spot because spots spread as they travel. The Rf value has no unit because it is one distance divided by another, and it must lie between zero and one because a spot cannot travel further than the solvent carrying it. To identify substances, the unknown sample is run alongside reference substances on the same paper in the same solvent. A spot in the sample at the same height as a reference spot is evidence that the sample contains that substance. This comparison must be made in the same solvent because different compounds have different Rf values in different solvents. The chromatogram also shows purity, since a pure substance produces a single spot while a mixture produces several.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The two phases.** The **stationary phase** does not move — in paper chromatography, the **paper**. The **mobile phase** is the **solvent**, moving through it.

**How separation happens.** It **depends on the distribution of substances between the phases**. A substance more attracted to the **mobile** phase spends more time moving, so travels **far**; one more attracted to the **stationary** phase stays **near the start**. Different substances distribute differently, so they end up in different places.

**The Rf value:**

$$R_f = \frac{\text{distance moved by the substance}}{\text{distance moved by the solvent}}$$

Measured to the **centre** of the spot, because spots spread. It has **no unit** and is always **between 0 and 1** — a spot cannot outrun the solvent carrying it.

**Identifying substances.** Run the unknown **alongside references**, on the **same paper in the same solvent**. A spot level with a reference is evidence for that substance. The same-solvent condition matters because **different compounds have different Rf values in different solvents**.

**And purity comes free:** **one spot** means a pure substance; **several** mean a mixture.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between the chemical and everyday meanings of the word pure, and describe how melting point data can be used to test purity.
questions.solution: The word pure carries two different meanings. In chemistry a pure substance is a single element or compound, not mixed with any other substance. In everyday language a pure substance is one that has had nothing added to it, so that it is unadulterated and in its natural state. These meanings can disagree. Milk sold as pure milk is pure in the everyday sense, because nothing has been added to it, but to a chemist it is not pure at all, since it is a mixture of water, fats, proteins and sugars. Both uses are correct within their own context, and questions on this point are testing whether the distinction is understood. Purity in the chemical sense can be tested using melting point and boiling point data, because pure elements and compounds melt and boil at specific temperatures. A pure substance therefore melts sharply at a single temperature, whereas a mixture melts gradually over a range of temperatures and does so at a lower temperature than the pure substance would. The same applies to boiling, with a mixture boiling over a range and at a higher temperature. So if a sample is found to melt sharply at one hundred and thirteen degrees Celsius it is pure, whereas a second sample melting between one hundred and five and one hundred and ten degrees is impure. The great advantage of this test is that it works without any knowledge of what the substance actually is, since it depends only on the shape of the melting behaviour rather than on the identity of the material.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Two meanings of one word:**

- **In chemistry**: a **single element or compound**, not mixed with anything else.
- **In everyday language**: **nothing has been added** — unadulterated, in its natural state.

**Where they disagree.** *Pure milk* is pure in the everyday sense but is a **mixture** of water, fats, proteins and sugars — so not pure at all to a chemist. Both uses are correct in their own context.

**Testing purity with melting point.** **Pure elements and compounds melt and boil at specific temperatures.**

| | Pure substance | Mixture |
|---|---|---|
| melting | one **sharp** temperature | over a **range**, and **lower** |
| boiling | one sharp temperature | over a range, and **higher** |

So a sample melting sharply at **113 °C** is pure; one melting between **105 and 110 °C** is impure.

**The mark most often missed** is *lower* — a mixture melts over a range **and** below the pure substance's melting point.

**And the reason the test is so useful:** it works **without knowing what the substance is**, since it depends on the shape of the melting behaviour rather than the identity of the material.

examTechnique.body:
Define a mixture as substances not chemically combined.

Give both meanings of pure when the question is about everyday language.

Say that a mixture melts over a range and at a lower temperature than the pure substance.

Identify a formulation by its designed components, measured quantities and required properties.

Measure chromatography distances from the origin to the centre of each spot.

Check that every Rf value lies between 0 and 1.

Compare Rf values only against references run in the same solvent.

Remember that one spot means a pure substance and several mean a mixture.
examinerErrors: Calling pure milk a pure substance in the chemical sense.
Saying a mixture melts over a range without saying it melts lower.
Describing an alloy as a compound.
Giving an Rf value greater than 1 without noticing it is impossible.
Measuring to the edge of a spot rather than its centre.
Identifying a substance from an Rf value alone, without a reference.
Giving a unit for an Rf value.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer holds both meanings of pure at once and can say which is being used. It gives the melting behaviour of a mixture in full, range and lower temperature together, and it recognises that this test works without knowing what the substance is. It treats a formulation as a designed mixture with three identifying features rather than as a list of examples, and it knows an alloy qualifies. On chromatography it explains separation through distribution between the phases, knows Rf cannot exceed 1 and why, and understands that an Rf value is evidence only when compared with a reference in the same solvent.
